reference.source: Movement-disorder and neurogenetics textbooks with peer-reviewed reviews
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant NBIA subtype caused by variants (typically insertions) in FTL, encoding the ferritin light chain
One of the few dominantly inherited NBIA disorders, usually presenting in adulthood
Phenotype is dominated by an extrapyramidal movement disorder: chorea, dystonia (often orofacial or action-specific), and parkinsonism, frequently asymmetrical at onset
Characteristic orolingual and facial dystonia may cause dysarthria and can resemble Huntington disease
Cognition is relatively preserved until late, in contrast to many other neurodegenerative movement disorders
Serum ferritin may be low or low-normal, particularly in affected males, providing a useful clue
MRI with iron-sensitive sequences shows iron in the basal ganglia and dentate nuclei and may reveal cystic cavitation of the putamen and globus pallidus in advanced disease
Diagnosis is confirmed by FTL molecular testing in the context of the imaging and family history; management is symptomatic
reference.pathophysiology: Neuroferritinopathy is caused by dominant variants in FTL, the gene for the ferritin light chain, most commonly small insertions that disrupt the carboxy-terminus of the protein. The abnormal ferritin has impaired capacity to sequester iron safely, so iron and abnormal ferritin aggregates accumulate within neurons and glia, particularly in the basal ganglia and cerebellar dentate nuclei. The resulting iron-mediated oxidative stress and inclusion formation drive progressive neurodegeneration, and advanced disease may lead to tissue cavitation within the affected deep grey-matter structures.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic torsion dystonia and other adult-onset dystonias
Young-onset Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism
Benign hereditary chorea and other choreiform syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with iron-sensitive sequences to demonstrate basal ganglia and dentate iron and any putaminal/pallidal cavitation
FTL molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Serum ferritin, which may be low, along with iron studies
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease and aceruloplasminaemia
Detailed family history and consideration of testing at-risk relatives given dominant inheritance
redFlags: Severe or disabling generalised chorea or dystonia
Bulbar dysfunction with dysphagia and aspiration risk
Rapid functional decline or new significant cognitive or psychiatric change
reference.prognosis: The disorder is slowly progressive over years to decades, with worsening movement disorder and eventual loss of independence, although cognition is often comparatively spared. Prognosis and rate of progression vary between affected individuals and families.
pitfalls: Diagnosing Huntington disease on clinical grounds without pursuing NBIA imaging and FTL testing when the huntingtin expansion is negative
Overlooking a low serum ferritin as a diagnostic clue
Failing to obtain iron-sensitive MRI sequences that reveal the deep grey-matter iron and cavitation
Not recognising the dominant inheritance and missing the opportunity for family counselling
management: There is no proven disease-modifying therapy, so treatment is directed symptomatically at the extrapyramidal movement disorder
Treat chorea with a dopamine-depleting agent such as tetrabenazine or with a dopamine-receptor antagonist
Manage dystonia with agents such as anticholinergics, baclofen or clonazepam, and consider botulinum toxin for focal orolingual or facial dystonia
Offer a trial of levodopa for parkinsonian features, recognising the response is variable
Approach iron chelation cautiously as it is unproven and may worsen anaemia and neurological status
Provide speech and language therapy for dysarthria and swallowing, physiotherapy for mobility and occupational therapy support
Refer to neurology movement-disorder services and clinical genetics, offering genetic counselling and predictive testing for at-risk relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
